paragraphs: §1 — Disputes of the present-day Karaites: the Sabbath

Among them is one who forbids washing from impurity on the day of the Sabbath; one who does not hold that he may wash his face on the Sabbath; one who does not hold the setting out of the dish on the Sabbath, nor the spreading of the bed — if he wishes to eat food, he draws close to where the food is until he eats it. Among them is one who holds the setting out of the dish and the spreading of the bed [permissible] but does not hold their removal [permissible], since setting out the dish and spreading the bed are for the need of the Sabbath, while removing them has no need for the Sabbath.

Among them is one who does not hold the wearing of the "takkah" (the drawing-up of the trousers) on the Sabbath. Among them is one who holds that he may do on the Sabbath what he will use after the Sabbath, of what is permitted to be done on the Sabbath for the Sabbath — such as cooling water and the like; this belongs to some of the Baghdadis.

Among them is one who does not hold that food may be left in its heat until the entry of the Sabbath, but [holds that] he should cool it before the entry of the Sabbath, claiming that if it remains hot, there falls upon it on the Sabbath an act, an increase, and a diminution; this belongs to some of the Tustarīs. And among them is one who denies this and holds also the keeping of [food] hot in the oven to eat it on the Sabbath. Among them is one who does not permit cooking and baking on any of the festivals except the Passover alone, claiming that the permission applies to it and not to another. It has reached me that some Tustarīs have lately [arisen] who permit on the festival only what is permitted on the Sabbath, claiming that the saying of Scripture [Exod 12:16] "אַךְ אֲשֶׁר יֵאָכֵל לְכָל נֶפֶשׁ" resembles His saying [Exod 16:25] "אִכְלֻהוּ הַיּוֹם."
§2 — The new barley, the ʿeruv, the sighting

Among them is one who holds [the festival] by the moist new-barley; one who does not take the month of the new-barley until the standing-grain (jirf) is found in all the land of the Children of Israel; one who takes [it] if the reaping was completed in a single plot (qarāḥ); and one who does this by [mere] inclining [of the ear toward ripeness].

Among them is one who does not hold carrying-out [of objects] on the Sabbath; one who does not hold the carrying-out from the place in which he sits to another inhabited place either, even if there is between the two places no courtyard and no partition; and one who holds [it permissible]. Among them is one who holds the wearing of a ring on the Sabbath, and one who does not — and not on a festival either.

Among them is one who permits the statement of "one [witness]" regarding the sighting of the new moon, and one who permits it only by two witnesses. Some of the Baghdadis used to take the new-barley by a place in Baghdad — claiming that he had [thereby] intercalated it, and that it stands for the Holy Land. Among them is one who, if he sought the moon on the twenty-ninth and did not see it, then saw it after that, took the head of the month on that day; and one who does not hold this.

Among them is one who follows the Exilarch in the intercalation of the day in [both] the Passover and the Festival of Booths together; one who follows him in this for the Passover but not for the Festival of Booths. Among them is one who follows "ʿAnan" also in the prohibition of circumcision on the day of the Sabbath, though most of them permit it.
§3 — Unleavened bread, the aṣīl, the Sabbath, slaughter, fish

Among them is one who holds that if he did not eat unleavened bread on any of the seven days, he transgresses — after [the rule that] he must not eat leaven; and one who makes its eating obligatory every day. Among them is one who claims that the time of the aṣīl is the whole of the [present] day; one who claims it is the whole of the morrow; and one who claims it is of the [present] day and of the morrow — following what "ʿAnan" said. Among them is one who holds that once the sun has set the Sabbath has gone out; and one who does not bring it out until the light has faded. Among them is one who permits reading any script other than Hebrew on the day of the Sabbath; and one who does not permit this. Among them is one who permits eating the flesh of sheep and cattle in the exile; and one who does not.

Among them is one who permits eating the fish that died in the hands of the dissenters; and one who does not. Among them is one who holds eating the scalded kid (gedi ḥalūṭ); and one who does not, claiming that the fat is cooked with it. Among them is one who holds eating the slaughter of the majority, and one who does not permit it. Among them is one who permits the saʿīr (rooster?), one who forbids it, and one who claimed he does not know whether it is permitted or forbidden.
§4 — Impurity, prayer, the head of the month

Among them is one who holds [the rule of] "a single intermediary" in impurity, claiming that this is [the right view]; one who holds "several intermediaries"; and one who holds no intermediary at all. Among them is one who makes the midday prayer obligatory every day; and one who holds it only on a fast-day. Among them is one who claims that if the Passover fell on a Sabbath eve, it must be transferred to the second month.

Among them is one who holds washing from impurity in hot water, and one who does not. Among them is one who holds washing from impurity only in fresh water (ʿadhb), and one who holds it only in living water.

The ancient Karaites of the Baṣrans claimed that the Festival of Weeks is only [on] a Sunday, but did not know which Sunday; and among them were some who claimed that it lapses in this age; and among them, too, were some who claimed that all the festivals lapse in this age, being only a "remembrance."

Some of the Syrian Karaites held that a man may fast from one thing and not another in the voluntary fast. Some of the Khurasanian Karaites forbid the "written and the read" (the qere and the ketiv), reading only what is written; and of these is one who does so with the Name (of glory), [reading] it as "Yāh Hāh," claiming that whoever reads it as "Adonai" has [thereby] disbelieved.
§5 — The Karaites of Khurasan; the dead; shoes on the Sabbath

Among the Karaites of Khurasan and the mountains is one who claims that the promised Messiah has already come and gone, and that the House, too, is the one Zerubbabel built, none other remaining. Of these, too, is one who annuls the resurrection of the dead, claiming that what Scripture reported of this was meant [as] the revival of the nation from the exile and from abasement.

Some of the Baghdadis claimed that Enoch and Elijah have already died, and that they may not have ascended to heaven in their bodies. Of the "innovators" among them are men of the Baṣrans and the Tustarīs who claimed that wearing the sandal and the belt without need is forbidden on the Sabbath; and likewise wearing more than one tunic, and the cloak (ridāʾ), and everything that need does not lead one to wear, such as the girdle (zunnār) and the like.

Among them is one who holds extinguishing the fire on the Sabbath if he had set it to do so before the Sabbath — rather, he makes it obligatory. Likewise they make obligatory the stopping of the water that irrigates the sown field on the Sabbath, if he had set it to be stopped before the Sabbath; and likewise they close the mill on the day of the Sabbath, [for] some such [reason], so that it not grind on the Sabbath. The wonder is that they permit — indeed make obligatory — acts and motions on the Sabbath, and forbid abstention and rest.
§6 — Further doubts and summary

They dissented over "doubtful cases" (shukūk), some making them obligatory and some not. They dissented over the contracting of the light impurity by the grave impurity: some held it obligatory, some not. They dissented over the impurity of a house from the corpse: some held it, some not. They dissented over one who let the fixed time of washing — which Scripture made obligatory — pass: some permitted him to wash at any time he wished, and some permitted it only at a comparable time. They dissented over the dwelling of strangers in the booth: some held it obligatory, some not.
§7 — Conclusion and closing blessing

These are what came to mind to record of their dissension; and the matter is increasing every day. It may be that one of our own people who reads this will blame his [own] memory for it — for there are among the Rabbanites those who reproach us with it, doing so under our reproaching of them with the dissension between the people of al-Shām and the people of Iraq. So let not [the Rabbanites] busy your hearts with this, nor turn to it. For it is they upon whom the disgrace and contradiction fell in this — only from the place where they claimed that all that is in their hands is transmitted from prophecy. What is of this kind may admit of no dissension at all; and in the falling of dissension is a refutation of the statement of whoever claims this. As for us — we bring forth knowledge by deriving it with our intellects; and what is of this kind, we do not deny that dissension may fall upon it. We shall later recount what the "dissenters" — of the obligation of reflection — claim from this angle, and the answer to it.
May this discourse be brought to completion by the help of God and His power.
Blessed be the Lord forever; Amen and Amen.
: This shows the extremity of Karaite Sabbath-scrupulosity in the exile: not only is setting out vessels forbidden, but one who spreads his own bed is reckoned a Sabbath-profaner.
: Arabic jirf, the standing barley (the ʿomer); the view that the spring festival (Passover) is fixed not by calendar but by the ripening of the barley in all the Land (and not part of it).
: A single witness for the sighting of the moon — the radical Karaite view requiring only one witness, against the rabbinic requirement of two (B. Rosh ha-Shanah 22b).
: The anti-rabbinic Karaite permission to read non-Hebrew texts on the Sabbath. Cf. Lieberman, Sheqiʿin, on the rabbinic prohibition of reading secular books on the Sabbath.
: "scalded kid" — a kid plunged into boiling water before slaughter; the question is whether it is then permitted to eat.
: Arabic saʿīr (rooster?); the term is obscure.
: "one intermediary" / "several intermediaries" — a technical dispute on impurity: whether a single vessel, or several, separates the impure from the pure.
: A distinctive view: if Passover falls on a Sabbath eve, it must be intercalated to the second month — a radical calendar ruling.
: The Yudghanite view (cf. bab 12) adopted by some Karaites — that all festivals lapse in the age of exile. Cf. Erder on the cross-influence of these currents.
: Arabic yāʾ hāʾ, an abbreviation of the Tetragrammaton; the view that the Name must be read as written and not substituted by "Adonai" — an anti-traditional, literalist position.

: An anti-traditional, realized-eschatology view: the Messiah has already come, and the "House" to be built in the future is Zerubbabel's Temple. Such views resemble messianic currents near the Mourners of Zion.
: Arabic ridāʾ, a cloak/mantle.
: Arabic zunnār, a modest girdle; extreme Karaites forbade it on the Sabbath, per Q.
: "doubtful cases" (shukūk), the adjudication of unclear cases. Cf. Frank, Search Scripture Well, on the Karaite handling of "doubts."

: Q's closing thesis: we [Karaites] bring forth knowledge by our intellects, so dissension among us is no contradiction. The Rabbanites — if they claim a received tradition — have every dispute among them annul that claim. This is Q's polemical epistemology, the declaration of Karaite difference from the Rabbanites. Cf. Chiesa, Filologia storica, on the structure of Q's epistemology.
